newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy urges balanced NATO expansion, backs Romania.
newsitem.headline: Italy urges balanced NATO expansion, backs Romania.

text.p: Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta, speaking after meeting his Romanian counterpart on Wednesday, called for a balanced expansion of NATO in the former Warsaw Pact and gave firm backing to Bucharest's bid to join.

"Italy has a strong interest in a re-balancing of the new entrants between the centre and south of Europe and...the participation of Romania in the alliance as soon as possible," Andreatta told a news conference with Romania's Victor Babiuc.
He said Italy was trying to balance an overly centrist notion of NATO enlargement, which is expected to begin at a summit of the 16 member nations in Madrid in July.
Babiuc, whose country can already count on high-level support from France, thanked Italy for its backing.
"Italy is a strong voice in Europe and this alliance and can influence it in a decisive way," he said.
"Romania thinks it has a real chance of entering in the first group," Babiuc said. "We are sure we deserve (it)."
Babiuc said Bucharest had estimated the cost of joining would be $9 billion but being left out would cost "much more".

Romania plans to entrust exiled King Michael with a mission to woo support for speedy NATO entry alongside Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic which are expected to be invited to join the alliance's first eastward expansion at the July summit.
NATO's plans to re-draw the Cold War military map with the ambitious enlargement have hit Russian opposition but alliance sources in Brussels said on Tuesday progress was being made.

Russia is pushing for a legally binding document on its relations with the alliance to allay its security fears but NATO wants a more flexible political commitment. Any final document could be ratified by heads of state and government in Madrid.
Andreatta likened NATO's challenges to those of concluding the Versailles peace treaty after World War One.
He said Italy strongly supported the entry of Slovenia in the first wave of NATO expansion, partly because that way there would be an uninterrupted geographical link between new members.
Senior officials said Italy also believed Slovakia was ready for NATO membership.
